title: Sasanian Mesopotamia
subtitle: 224–637 AD · The Heart of Ērānšahr — Ctesiphon the Imperial Capital, the Nahrawan and the Richest Land on Earth, the Church of the East and the Talmud, and the Arab Conquest

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Ardashir making the Sawad the empire's core, Shapur I and the captured Roman emperors, Shapur II's long war, the fifth-century disasters, Kavad and Mazdak, Khosrow I's great reforms, Khosrow II's last war, and the Arab conquest

entries.label: Ardashir I and the making of the Sawad
entries.hint: Ardashir destroyed the last Arsacid in 224, was crowned at Ctesiphon in 226, took Hatra around 240, and built a centralised empire — Ērānšahr, 'the domain of the Iranians' — where the Parthians had held a loose confederation. He kept the capital at Ctesiphon and made lowland Mesopotamia, the Sawad, the empire's directly-ruled core and its richest province. It stayed the heart of the state for four hundred years.
entries.note: al-Tabari I (tr. Bosworth 1999); the 'Kārnāmag ī Ardaxšīr'; Touraj Daryaee, 'Sasanian Persia' (2009).

entries.label: Shapur I and the captured emperors
entries.hint: Shapur I beat three Roman emperors — Gordian III died on campaign in 244, Philip bought peace, and Valerian was taken alive near Edessa in 260 and kept as a living trophy. Shapur cut the great trilingual record of it into the rock at Naqsh-e Rostam, and resettled the tens of thousands he deported from Antioch and Syria in new cities near Ctesiphon and at Gondeshapur.
entries.note: the 'Res Gestae Divi Saporis' (the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht inscription); the Naqsh-e Rostam reliefs; Michael Dodgeon & Samuel Lieu, 'The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars' (1991).

entries.label: Shapur II — the long war and the first persecution
entries.hint: Shapur II reigned seventy years. He won back the districts Rome had taken in 298, failed three times to storm Nisibis, and in 363 trapped the Emperor Julian's invasion below Ctesiphon; Julian died in the retreat and the treaty handed Persia Nisibis, Singara and five provinces. From 340 he ran the empire's first great persecution of Christians, now suspected as agents of a Christian Rome.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus XVIII–XXV; Sozomen, 'Ecclesiastical History' II.9–14 on the persecution; the 'Acts of the Persian Martyrs'.

entries.label: The fifth-century kings and the Hephthalite disaster
entries.hint: A century of mixed fortune: Yazdegerd I made peace with Rome and eased the pressure on the Christians, letting them organise a church; his son Bahram V, raised among the Arabs of al-Hira, is the huntsman-king of Persian legend. Then the eastern nomads, the Hephthalites, broke the empire's army and killed King Peroz in 484, forcing years of tribute and destabilising the throne.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; the Synod of 410 acts (Yazdegerd I); Procopius, 'Wars' I.3–4 on Peroz and the Hephthalites.

entries.label: Kavad I and the Mazdakite crisis
entries.hint: Kavad backed — or used — the preacher Mazdak, whose movement demanded the sharing out of wealth and undercut the nobles and the clergy. The establishment deposed and jailed him in 496; he escaped to the Hephthalites and came back with an army to reclaim the throne. His son Khosrow ended the affair by massacring the Mazdakites, and inherited a nobility that had been badly frightened.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; Patricia Crone, 'Kavad's Heresy and Mazdak's Revolt' (Iran 1991).

entries.label: Khosrow I Anushirvan — the great reforms
entries.hint: Khosrow I rebuilt the state on the ruins Mazdak left. He had the Sawad surveyed field by field and replaced the crop-share with a fixed cash tax; he broke the great nobles' military monopoly by paying and equipping a royal cavalry and splitting the command four ways; and he built a court culture — the translations, Gondeshapur, the Book of Kings. He also sacked Antioch in 540 and deported it wholesale.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; Procopius, 'Wars' II; Zeev Rubin, 'The Reforms of Khusro Anushirwan' (1995).

entries.label: Khosrow II Parviz and the last great war
entries.hint: Khosrow II overran the whole Roman East — Syria, Jerusalem and the True Cross in 614, Egypt by 619, an army at the walls of Constantinople in 626. Then Heraclius marched the other way, through Armenia and down into the Sawad, won at Nineveh in 627, and burned the royal palace at Dastagird. Khosrow was overthrown and killed by his own son in 628, and the dynasty fell into four years of coups.
entries.note: the 'Chronicon Paschale'; Theophylact Simocatta; Walter Kaegi, 'Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium' (2003).

entries.label: Asōristān — the heart of Ērānšahr
entries.hint: Lowland Mesopotamia was the province the Persians called Asōristān and, in a phrase the sources use, 'the heart of Ērānšahr'. It held the capital, the greatest concentration of people and irrigated land in the empire, and by the seventh century it yielded well over half the crown's cash revenue. It was ruled directly through the court, not farmed out to a vassal — the one indispensable province.
entries.note: the 'Šahrestānīhā ī Ērānšahr'; Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984); the tax figures in al-Tabari and Ibn Khurradadhbih.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Shapur's three triumphs over Rome and the fall of Hatra, the Roman counterstroke and the peace of 298, Julian's death before Ctesiphon, the sack of Antioch, Heraclius in the Sawad, and al-Qadisiyya and the fall of the capital

entries.label: Shapur's three triumphs and the fall of Hatra
entries.hint: Ardashir took Hatra around 240 and razed the shrine-city that had twice held off Rome. His son Shapur then won the greatest run of victories any Persian king ever had over Rome: a dead emperor in 244, a bought peace, the storm of Antioch, and in 260 the capture of the Emperor Valerian himself with his army near Edessa. The Palmyrene Odaenathus, not Rome, drove Shapur back to Ctesiphon.
entries.note: the 'Res Gestae Divi Saporis'; the Bishapur and Naqsh-e Rostam reliefs; Dodgeon & Lieu (1991).

entries.label: The Roman counterstroke and the peace of 298
entries.hint: The Emperor Carus sacked Ctesiphon in 283, and in 298 Galerius routed King Narseh, captured his harem and treasury, and dictated terms: Rome took five provinces east of the Tigris and made Nisibis the sole legal crossing-point for trade. It was the high-water mark of Roman Mesopotamia, and it held for sixty years until Shapur II tore it up.
entries.note: the 'Panegyrici Latini'; Peter Brennan on the Treaty of Nisibis; Ammianus XXV.

entries.label: Julian dies before Ctesiphon
entries.hint: The Emperor Julian brought an army of sixty thousand down the Euphrates to end the Persian problem for good. He beat the defenders under the walls of Ctesiphon but could not take the city, burned his own boats, and turned back up the Tigris harried the whole way. A skirmish wound killed him on 26 June; his successor Jovian bought the army's escape by ceding Nisibis and the five provinces.

entries.label: The sack of Antioch and the deportation
entries.hint: Breaking the 'Eternal Peace' of 532, Khosrow I marched into Syria in 540, stormed Antioch, and carried its whole population back east to a new city he built for them beside Ctesiphon — 'Khosrow's Better-than-Antioch' — with its own hippodrome and its own bath. The great cities of the Roman East learned that the peace on the frontier was only ever a pause.
entries.note: Procopius, 'Wars' II.8–14; the deportee city in al-Tabari I and the Arabic 'al-Rumiyya'.

entries.label: Heraclius in the Sawad
entries.hint: After twenty years in which Khosrow II conquered the entire Roman East, the Emperor Heraclius gambled everything on a strike at the Persian core. He came through Armenia, wintered in Albania, and in December 627 destroyed the last Persian field army on the old battlefield of Nineveh, then burned Khosrow's palace at Dastagird. The king was murdered weeks later. Both empires were now bankrupt and exhausted.

entries.label: al-Qadisiyya and the fall of Ctesiphon
entries.hint: Arab columns raided lower Iraq from 633; al-Hira submitted at once. In November 636, on the desert edge near al-Qadisiyya, a three-day battle destroyed the main Persian army and killed its commander Rustam. Ctesiphon — al-Madā'in — fell the following spring, its treasury and the great vault taken; the rout at Nihavand in 642 ended organised resistance. The last king fled east and was murdered in 651.
entries.note: al-Tabari I (tr. Friedmann 1992, 'The Battle of al-Qādisiyyah'); al-Baladhuri, 'Futūh al-Buldān'.
